lead: Both readings speak of a new birth and a new life. Colossians tells the baptized to put off the old self like a garment and put on the new, renewed in the image of the Creator, where Christ is all and in all. In John, Nicodemus comes by night and hears that no one can enter the kingdom of God without being born of water and Spirit. The Easter season is the season of Baptism, and today’s readings explain what happened at the font.

set: The letter is written in the name of Paul to the Church at Colossae in Asia Minor. Many scholars think it was written by a disciple of Paul after his lifetime; others hold that Paul wrote it, perhaps through a co-worker. The Church reads it as part of the apostolic witness. Just before this reading the letter says, “you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (3:3). Today’s verses draw the consequences: because you have been raised with Christ, live accordingly.
str: vv. 5–7: put to death what is earthly: a first list of vices.
vv. 8–9a: get rid of sins of anger and the tongue: a second list.
vv. 9b–10: the old self stripped off, the new self put on.
v. 11: in the new creation the old divisions fall away: Christ is all and in all.
kw: A strong word. Baptism has already joined us to Christ’s death (2:12); now that death must be carried into daily life.
Literally “wanting more”. The letter calls it idolatry, because whatever we crave above God takes the place of God.
The language of changing clothes. Early Christian Baptism made it visible: the candidate took off old clothes, went down into the water, and was clothed in a white garment.
vv: Put to death, therefore, whatever in you is earthly:
“Earthly” does not mean the body or the material world, which God made good. It means the old life turned away from God.
On account of these the wrath of God is coming on those who are disobedient.
Textual note: the words “on those who are disobedient” are missing in some of the oldest manuscripts and may have come in from Ephesians 5:6. The POC follows the shorter text.
and have clothed yourselves with the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge according to the image of its creator.
An echo of Genesis 1:27. In Christ, the true image of God (1:15), the image in which we were made is restored.
In that renewal there is no longer Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave and free; but Christ is all and in all!
A “barbarian” was anyone who did not speak Greek; the Scythians, from north of the Black Sea, were the byword for the uncivilized. None of these labels decides a person’s worth in Christ.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Baptism makes the neophyte “a new creature”, an adopted son of God, a member of Christ (CCC 1265). The white garment given at Baptism, still part of our rite, shows that the baptized person has “put on Christ” (Galatians 3:27; CCC 1243). The conversion begun at the font continues through the whole Christian life (CCC 1428).

set: Nicodemus is a Pharisee and “a leader of the Jews”, a member of the ruling council. He comes by night, perhaps for safety, perhaps for quiet study; in John, night is also the darkness from which a person comes toward the light (3:19–21). He appears twice more: defending Jesus’ right to a hearing (7:50–51) and bringing spices for his burial (19:39). He is a man who slowly comes into the light.
str: vv. 1–2: Nicodemus comes by night: “we know that you are a teacher who has come from God.”
v. 3: Jesus: to see the kingdom, one must be born from above.
vv. 5–8: born of water and Spirit; flesh and spirit; the wind.
kw: The Greek means both. Jesus means “from above”, from God; Nicodemus hears “again”. Both are true: it is a second birth, and it comes from God. The POC renders it “again”.
The Church has always heard Baptism in these words: the water is the sign, the Spirit gives the life.
The same Greek word means both. Jesus plays on it in v. 8: you hear the wind and cannot see it; so it is with the Spirit and those born of him.
vv: He came to Jesus by night
He comes as a teacher to a teacher. He will learn that this is not a matter of better teaching but of new birth.
Very truly, I tell you, no one can see the kingdom of God without being born from above.
Jesus does not answer Nicodemus’s compliment; he answers his need.
Very truly, I tell you, no one can enter the kingdom of God without being born of water and Spirit.
The Church’s classic text on the necessity of Baptism. God has bound salvation to Baptism, but he himself is not bound by his sacraments (CCC 1257).
So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.
The life of the Spirit cannot be controlled or predicted, but its effects can be seen, as the trees bend under the wind.
ch: The Catechism cites this Gospel when it explains that Baptism is called “the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit”, because it brings about the birth of water and the Spirit without which no one can enter the kingdom of God (CCC 1215). The Fathers delighted in the image of the font as the womb of Mother Church, where children are born of water and the Spirit.

study: Colossians names greed as idolatry. What do I want “more” of, so that it competes with God in my heart?
Nicodemus came by night and slowly came into the light. Where am I still coming to Jesus “by night”, privately and with caution?
